title: When Three Purchases Go in a Circle — Samuelson’s (1938) Revealed Preference, Houthakker & Afriat’s GARP Cycle Theorem & Choi’s Experimental Budget-Line Tests of Rational Choice Under Risk

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: Can we tell if a shopper's choices follow a consistent preference map without ever peeking inside their head? Samuelson and Afriat proved that if three purchases form a budget-violating cycle, no utility function can rationalize them—tested cleanly in Choi's risk lab.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Revealed preference turns abstract 'rationality' into concrete, testable inequalities on real household and experimental budget data.
keyTakeaways: Samuelson's Weak Axiom says if bundle A was chosen when B was strictly affordable, B cannot later be chosen when A is strictly affordable.

Houthakker and Afriat's Theorem proved that finite price-quantity data can be generated by a nonsatiated concave utility function if and only if they satisfy the Generalized Axiom of Revealed Preference (GARP)—no preference cycles.
Afriat's Critical Cost Efficiency Index (CCEI) measures how close noisy human choices come to consistency (e.g., 0.95 means budgets need only a 5% shrink to break every cycle).

vocab.meaning: Generalized Axiom of Revealed Preference—ruling out any cycle A >= B >= ... >= Z where Z is strictly cheaper at A's prices.
Equivalence between zero GARP violations in finite price-bundle data and existence of a well-behaved utility function rationalizing all choices.
Afriat's Critical Cost Efficiency Index in (0, 1], quantifying severity of GARP violations.

quiz.question: What does an Afriat Critical Cost Efficiency Index (CCEI) of 1.00 indicate about a consumer's observed budget choices?
options: Zero GARP cycles exist, so a nonsatiated utility function can rationalize 100% of the observed choices
quiz.explanation: CCEI = 1 means budgets require zero shrinkage to eliminate revealed-preference cycles.
